candidates.original_title: Tact training versus bidirectional intraverbal training in teaching a foreign language
candidates.description: The original study tested the effects of foreign tact and bidirectional intraverbal training on emergent verbal relations in teaching a foreign language vocabulary to adults.
candidates.citation_sentence: The present study aimed to replicate the findings of Dounavi (Journal of Applied Behavior Analysis, 47(1), 165–170 2014)
candidates.notes: The authors explicitly state they replicated Dounavi (2014) and the results confirm the original findings: foreign tact and N-F intraverbal training were more effective than F-N training. Minor methodological refinements (added N-F baseline probe, no feedback during probes, counterbalanced posttraining probes, added third participant, added 4-week follow-up) do not change the direct replication classification. The paper reports a successful direct replication of Dounavi (2014) with minor methodological refinements (added N-F baseline probe, no feedback during probes, counterbalanced posttraining probes, added a third participant, added 4-week follow-up). The discussion explicitly states 'The present study replicated Dounavi's (2014) research.' The original DOI was not found in the paper and is left blank.

candidates.original_title: Tact training versus bidirectional intraverbal training in teaching a foreign language
candidates.description: Foreign tact and native-to-foreign intraverbal training are more effective than foreign-to-native intraverbal training in producing emergent verbal relations during foreign-language learning.
candidates.citation_sentence: The present study aims to further evaluate the efficacy of foreign tact versus bidirectional training in teaching a small foreign language vocabulary and facilitating emergent responding by systematically replicating Dounavi (2014).
candidates.notes: The study is explicitly described as a systematic replication, with deliberate procedural refinements including textual rather than vocal stimuli, fewer stimuli, an added participant, counterbalanced probes, and maintenance assessment.
